BCG’s 2026 survey of 65 chiefs of staff finds that AI is reshaping—not eliminating—the role. As technology takes over information-heavy coordination, CEOs have an opportunity to redeploy chiefs of staff toward the judgment, trust, and organizational influence that AI cannot reproduce.

The chief of staff extends the CEO’s impact, rather than merely managing timeMore than 70% of respondents cite execution and delivery as a primary focus, making the role a cross-functional force for turning leadership priorities into action.

AI is first automating preparation, then advancing the CEO’s agendaAI already saves time for 66% of chiefs of staff synthesizing decision materials; within two to three years, it is expected to streamline briefing, priority tracking, and initiative oversight.

Trust and judgment become more valuable as routine work recedesAI has limited reach in sensitive leadership relationships: only 20% expect it to reduce time spent motivating the organization. Confidentiality, political judgment, and credibility remain distinctly human work.

CEOs must deliberately give the role mandate, access, and authorityA clear mandate matters: 50% of chiefs of staff with one report being highly successful, versus 29% operating under loose expectations. Visible CEO backing turns formal scope into real influence.

Chiefs of staff arguably have the broadest portfolio in the executive suite, short of the CEO. Depending on the size and culture of the company, their responsibilities can stretch from managing day-to-day execution and keeping the CEO’s priorities on track to framing decisions, clarifying strategy, and being the CEO’s closest adviser. Chiefs of staff are executional in method and strategic in leverage: they earn standing by running things within their scope and create value by shaping what gets run.While AI is increasingly taking on parts of that broad portfolio—97% of the chiefs of staff BCG recently surveyed already use AI on the job—it is not replacing the CoS. To be sure, chiefs of staff expect that over the next two to three years, AI will take on more of the coordination and reconciliation of inconsistencies that consume their work today. It’s true that AI is reducing the time spent synthesizing information and preparing materials for boards and executive leadership teams. But AI is expected to have much less of an effect on the more human side of the job: exercising judgment and earning the trust to act on behalf of the CEO. Handling these sensitive conversations and complex people matters demands a level of maturity that technology simply cannot replicate.The real opportunity is to intentionally redirect the efficiency gained from AI into these high-stakes relationships. The potential payoff is greater than a more efficient CoS. AI can free chiefs of staff to take on responsibilities that bring enhanced value to the CEO. And as AI assumes more of the traditional chief-of-staff duties, that shift may become a necessity rather than simply an opportunity. The CEO must decide where the CoS can contribute greater value and provide the mandate and authority to do it.This article builds on BCG’s 2020 study of CEO support staff and its 2024 follow-up on finding and developing a chief of staff. The question now is not who to hire, but how to design the position as AI absorbs a growing share of its routine administrative and information synthesis responsibilities. To examine that issue, in a 2026 update BCG polled 65 chiefs of staff from across large companies, select unicorns, and nonprofits and supplemented our findings with in-depth interviews with survey respondents.Where Chiefs of Staff Create the Most Value
Chiefs of staff identified three areas where they believe they create the most value: driving the execution of strategic priorities, clarifying and amplifying strategy so that the CEO and leadership team stay focused on the same things, and improving decision quality by ensuring that the right information and framing arrive at the right moment. (See Exhibit 1.)

At least two-thirds of respondents ranked each in their top three, and driving execution drew the most first-place votes. Protecting and optimizing CEO time, a function often assumed to define the position, ranked among the top three for a small cohort—fewer than one in ten. In other words, the CoS creates value less by managing the CEO’s time and attention than by extending the CEO’s impact across the organization.The distinction is important. The CoS is not a senior executive assistant. Where an EA primarily oversees the CEO’s schedule and logistics, the CoS works through the organization on the CEO’s behalf, aligning priorities, securing cooperation, maintaining strategic and tactical quality standards, and ensuring that decisions are carried out. More than 70% of survey respondents named execution and delivery as a primary focus. Internal integration followed at 60%, with decision and information management and strategy and advisory at 57% each. In practice, that can mean ensuring that a CEO’s initiative actually gets implemented one day and helping frame a consequential decision the next. (See Exhibit 2.)

The shape of the CoS role bends around the makeup of the rest of the C-suite. In companies with chief strategy officers, only 42% of chiefs of staff said that strategy and giving advice are a primary focus of their job; in comparison, 71% of chiefs of staff without a CSO said the same. The presence of a COO produces another, similar shift: 67% identified execution and delivery as a primary focus compared with 86% without a COO. In organizations with both a chief of staff and a COO, chiefs of staff are typically focused on one- to five-year horizons rather than quarterly or annual performance and execution.Whatever the precise division of responsibilities, the CoS generally does not have a functional agenda in the way other C-suite executives do. That allows the CoS to work throughout the organization, across the company’s functions, serving as a neutral broker on the leadership team—“Switzerland,” as one chief of staff described it.AI Is Shifting the CoS Role’s Center of Gravity
The impact of AI on chiefs of staff is unfolding in stages. Information preparation is being affected substantially today. Advancing the CEO agenda is likely to yield to AI over the next two to three years. The relational side of the job—the responsibilities that depend most on judgment, trust, influence, and personal credibility—is expected to be far less affected by AI. (See Exhibit 3.)

Preparing Information and Materials: AI Is Already Reducing the Time Required. Even now, AI can take on much of the upfront work that occupies a CoS’s time. Sixty percent or more of chiefs of staff say AI is reducing the time they spend preparing board materials (60%), organizing and facilitating executive leadership team meetings (60%), and synthesizing information to frame decisions (66%). They expect AI’s impact in these areas to grow over the next two to three years, with more than 70% of respondents anticipating time savings in each. The point is not simply that AI can help the chief of staff do these things faster. By taking on more of these tasks, AI can free the CoS to focus on the decisions and judgment that follow and allow teams to apply suitable decision hygiene to AI-generated insights.Advancing the CEO’s Agenda: the Next Wave. AI’s next significant impact may be on the responsibilities that help the CEO’s agenda move through the organization. Only about a third of chiefs of staff said AI is reducing the time they spend briefing the CEO on key developments (34%) or ensuring that the CEO’s time aligns with organizational goals (32%). Over the next two to three years, 74% and 72%, respectively, believe AI will reduce the time these responsibilities require. A similar change is expected for overseeing the execution of CEO-led initiatives: 40% reported time savings from AI today, compared with 70% within two to three years.Again, that is a more consequential shift than simply tracking meetings and milestones faster. As AI takes on more of the groundwork necessary to keep the CEO’s priorities moving, the CoS can spend more time getting ahead of potential problems, resolving them before they impact the organization, and making sure that strategic plans are carried out.Relational Work: Where AI Has Less Reach. Chiefs of staff foresee much less impact from AI on the more relational parts of their job. Only 10% said AI currently reduces the time they spend inspiring and motivating the organization, and just 20% said they believe it will do so within two to three years. For managing leadership team relationships, the comparable figures are 30% and 34%. Acting as the CEO’s external extension shows no expected change at all, with 29% reporting an impact both today and in two to three years.There are good reasons for AI’s limited reach in areas like these. Building trust, exercising political judgment, and reading a room require soft skills that AI cannot readily replicate. These responsibilities can also involve sensitive conversations where confidentiality and discretion matter, placing further constraints on the role AI can play. One CoS described deliberately keeping AI note takers out of executive sessions because “that’s written on record, and sometimes you don’t necessarily want things to be written on record.” The most private rooms are often the ones AI is not invited into.

The Shift Won’t Happen by Itself
What makes a CoS effective is clear. Respondents identified strong stakeholder relationships (80%) as the leading contributor to their success, followed by CEO trust (55%) and prior experience (52%). (See Exhibit 4.) These are qualities and relationships that the CoS must develop.

By contrast, CEOs have a more direct role in removing the barriers that prevent chiefs of staff from succeeding. Asked what limits their effectiveness, chiefs of staff pointed to four conditions largely within the CEO’s control: a clear mandate, access to information, sufficient decision-making authority, and visible backing from the CEO. Most of these start with an unambiguous description of the scope and boundaries of the role.Mandate Clarity. Two-thirds of chiefs of staff said that an unclear or shifting mandate limits their effectiveness. Among those with a formal or clearly stated mandate, 50% described themselves as highly successful, compared with 29% of those operating with a looser understanding of the job. Yet only about half of chiefs of staff say they have such a mandate. As one put it, “The issue with the chief of staff role is that every organization has a different interpretation.” The CEO needs to establish a clear mandate for the CoS and make sure the rest of the organization understands not only what the position is responsible for but also where those responsibilities begin and end.Access to Information. Forty-two percent of chiefs of staff identified information parity as a constraint. The problem is particularly acute for chiefs of staff who participate in executive leadership team decisions: 47% cited inadequate access to information as a constraint, compared with 21% of those who do not. The more the CEO expects the CoS to participate in consequential decisions, the more important it becomes that the CoS sees what the CEO sees when the CEO sees it.The practical test is not whether the CoS feels informed. The CEO should be able to identify any forums and distribution lists from which the CoS is excluded—and explain why. And a disciplined process is necessary for briefing the CoS on information from bilateral conversations, where critical exchanges of essential insight often occur.Decision Rights. Twenty-eight percent of chiefs of staff said insufficient delegation limits their effectiveness: 37% of more junior chiefs of staff said so, versus 20% of those at the VP level or above.Interviews showed how wide this variance runs. One CoS routinely makes decisions on her CEO’s behalf, describing the freedom to anticipate his position and occasionally be wrong as essential to doing her job. Another reports the opposite in plain terms: “I’m not taking decisions off of his plate. He wants to be a decision maker.”Both approaches can work. The CEO’s responsibility is to make the boundaries clear and consistent. One CoS drew the line at capital, with routine calls delegated and anything approaching a $5 million commitment returning to the CEO.Visible Authority. A quarter of chiefs of staff (26%) said the CEO’s failure to sufficiently signal their authority to the leadership team limits their effectiveness. Not surprisingly, what the CEO says is less important than what the CEO does. For instance, CEOs can establish a CoS’s standing by visibly and repeatedly routing work through them, so that authority accrues from what colleagues observe. Teams mirror what the CEO tolerates, quickly noticing if a CoS can be bypassed. As one CoS put it, “Whatever role they want you to have, they should take action to show everyone in the org that you do have that role.” Another described what counts most more simply as “people seeing that he trusts me.”For CEOs: Is Your Chief of Staff Set Up for What Comes Next?
As the CoS position evolves, CEOs have more choices about how to design it—and more reasons to make those choices deliberately. These questions can help:Where could my CoS create greater value than today, and what responsibilities would need to change to make that possible?As AI takes on more of the tasks that occupy my CoS today, where could that capacity be put to greater use?Does my CoS have a clear mandate, and does the rest of the organization understand it?Does my CoS have access to the information needed to do the job I expect?Is it clear which decisions my CoS can make independently and which require my involvement?Have I made the CoS’s authority clear through my actions, not simply through what I say?Importantly, does my CoS believe that I am open to constructive skepticism and challenges to my way of thinking?Conclusion
There has never been a single model for an effective chief of staff. The position changes with the needs of the CEO, the composition of the leadership team, and the demands facing the organization. That flexibility has always been one of its strengths. But the job can also become burdened by responsibilities accumulated over time, making it harder for the CoS to adapt as circumstances change.AI adds a new reason—and an opportunity—to rethink the role, the communications around it, and the CEO’s support. As technology takes on more of what occupies chiefs of staff today, it creates room to reconsider how best to capitalize on their time and proximity to the CEO. Organizations can simply use AI to streamline the existing job, or they can seize the opportunity to align the position with the modern demands of the business and its evolving strategic priorities. The first produces a more efficient chief of staff. The second can result in a more consequential one.
